title: Isolating the impacts of stratification and eutrophication on interannual variability in coastal oxygen depletion
content:
Abstract

Effective hypoxia management requires disentangling natural (e.g., stratification) and anthropogenic (e.g., nutrient enrichment) drivers, which are often influenced by the same external factors, leading to temporally correlated effects. Here, we present a machine learning framework that integrates spatial monitoring data to enhance temporal analysis, enabling quantitative separation of stratification and eutrophication impacts on interannual oxygen depletion (measured as apparent oxygen utilization, AOU). We applied this framework to 29-year water quality data from 69 stations in the lower Pearl River Estuary. Our findings indicate that, during the entire period from 1995 to 2023, non-stratification factors (primarily eutrophication) dominate interannual variability in summer AOU, exerting 1.3 times (plume region) to 1.8 times (non-plume region) the influence of stratification. However, after 2007, a decline in the variability of eutrophication-related variables (e.g., turbidity and phosphate) leads to more stable interannual AOU fluctuations, shifting the primary driver of variability to stratification. Despite this stabilization, the persistently elevated AOU levels underscore an increased vulnerability to hypoxia. Furthermore, we identify a temporal shift in the factors controlling eutrophication variability: prior to 2007, light availability influenced by turbidity is dominant, while post-2007, nutrient levels (phosphate and nitrate) become more critical. Our framework also detects seasonal reversals in the dominance of these drivers (i.e., an increased role of stratification in early autumn than in summer), illustrating its flexibility across time scales. These findings enhance our understanding of interannual variability in coastal oxygen depletion and provide a transferable, data-driven approach for driver attribution in similarly monitored environments.
